title: The Accidental Architect of the Internet’s Brain
excerpt: Carson Griffith writes about Scott Pruitt, the most prolific super editor on Wikipedia, and the A.I. companies that lack the online encyclopedia’s human touch.
content_html:
Steven Pruitt, who is widely regarded as the most prolific Wikipedia editor, has made more than six million edits to the site, and, by extension, has quietly shaped the raw material that every major A.I. chatbot was trained on.

July 30, 2026

Steven Pruitt spends his evenings identifying errors that most people never notice and making fixes that hardly anyone ever thanks him for. He toils at a desk in a town house in Alexandria, Virginia, surrounded by books—the kind of working clutter that suggests a long relationship with paper rather than a fetish for screens. And yet his work is necessarily digital; after dinner, and sometimes late into the night, he uses his desktop computer to correct dates, clean up syntax, standardize categories, and occasionally write entire biographies of people on Wikipedia, the free online encyclopedia.

Wikipedia is not his employer, of course. Like all editors on the site, Pruitt is a volunteer. “At this point, I won’t say I don’t have any skin in the game,” he told me. “But it’s a lot lower stakes than a job because if I get something wrong, it’s fairly easy to fix it. I can fix it myself. I can do what I want to do on my own time.” Still, he holds himself to some rules: “I do try to get in at least one edit a day.”

Pruitt is forty-two, and works full time as a records-management contractor for the federal government. After graduating from the College of William & Mary, in 2006, he moved back in with his parents, owing to the cost of real estate in Alexandria. In recent years, he helped his mother care for his father. (While I was reporting this story, Pruitt’s father died.) In effect, Pruitt—the person who has done more than anyone else to shape the English-language Wikipedia—lives a life that is, by most outward measures, unremarkable.

According to public tallies, Pruitt has made more than six million edits to Wikipedia and created more than thirty thousand articles. He is widely regarded as the most prolific Wikipedian in the entire world. (“It depends on how you’re counting,” he said. “Different tools count different things.”) In 2017, Time magazine included him on its list of the most influential people on the internet. But outside of a small circle of editors, researchers, and obsessive readers on Wikipedia, the recognition has barely registered.

On the site, he is known by his username, Ser Amantio di Nicolao—a reference to a minor character in “Gianni Schicchi,” Giacomo Puccini’s comic opera. Pruitt’s interest in opera is genuine, but the flourish is misleading. He avoids drama, which means that he avoids writing Wikipedia biographies of people who are still alive, whenever possible. “I generally don’t do a lot in the realm of current events,” he told me. “Not just because the stakes are too high but sometimes because there’s so much editing going on on a subject in a particular moment that it can take me five or ten minutes just to break in with one edit.” He prefers biographies of what he calls “fairly obscure dead people.”

“They’re settled,” he explained.

In 2001, Jimmy Wales, an internet entrepreneur, and Larry Sanger, a philosopher, launched Wikipedia as an experiment in collaborative knowledge creation, allowing anyone with an internet connection to contribute. Pruitt first encountered the site in 2003, when he was still in college. “I didn’t quite understand what it was,” he recalled.

For more than a year, he did not edit at all. He would stumble upon Wikipedia pages through search results or links, and then move on. Between late 2004 and early 2005, though, his relationship to the site began to change. The encyclopedia had reached what he described as a critical mass: “There was enough stuff on the site that there was always something to do,” he said. “But it wasn’t just a blank slate.” The difference mattered. A completely empty encyclopedia was intimidating; a partially filled one invited correction and expansion.

Some of Pruitt’s first contributions were related to niche aspects of the Revolutionary War, including an entry on one of his own ancestors, a relatively obscure soldier from Virginia. He wrote several articles on topics and figures—such as Francis Salvador, the first Jew to be killed in the Revolutionary War—that would have been unlikely to appear in a traditional encyclopedia, and he watched, with a kind of amazement, as they remained, becoming permanent parts of the internet. “At this point, it’s over twenty years,” he said.

Pruitt was actively editing during Wikipedia’s first major growth spurt. In 2006, its English-language edition reached a million articles, a milestone that signalled both scale and legitimacy. (Wikipedia now exists in an estimated three hundred and forty-six languages, with the English edition containing the most entries.) As the site became bigger and more prominent, expectations hardened. Editing became less about authorship and more about stewardship. “Even if an article looks complete, honestly, it isn’t ever really complete,” Pruitt said. Every page existed in a state of provisionality, open to revision and dispute.

Over time, Pruitt’s work shifted away from creating new articles and toward improving existing ones. He standardized categories, repaired references, and corrected small errors before they crystallized into misinformation. He has still seen some of those errors migrate elsewhere on the internet. “You fix something,” he said, “and then you’ll see it show up years later somewhere else.”

Today, much of Pruitt’s work is made possible by a specialized editing tool called AutoWikiBrowser. It allows experienced users to make rapid, semi-automated edits across large numbers of articles, flagging common problems and applying standardized fixes. Pruitt uses it to revise at a scale that wouldn’t be possible by analog means: correcting dates, repairing broken links, standardizing citations, and cleaning up formatting across thousands of pages. Despite the name, “it’s not automatic,” he said. “You still have to review every edit.” The tool does not write articles or make judgments. It accelerates maintenance.

As I perched next to Pruitt in his den, he turned to the computer and began doing what he calls “mass editing.” He opened up a web-based external tool known as PetScan, which generates lists of Wikipedia articles by category, allowing him to layer categories the way a researcher might combine search terms. “Women scientists” crossed with “19th-century physicists,” for example, produces a list of biographies that fit both criteria, revealing pages that might be missing a relevant classification.

The method depends on intersections. Categories are layered together until they produce a set of pages that can be worked through in sequence. Too broad, and the list becomes unusable; too narrow, and it returns almost nothing. After Pruitt ran the query for “19th-century women physicists,” a list of articles appeared. From there, he moved quickly. He opened a biography and checked whether it had been categorized correctly. In some cases, an article about a nineteenth-century woman physicist had been tagged as a scientist but not as a physicist. Many entries required only small corrections; others needed more substantive changes. The work consisted of small decisions made in rapid succession, each one nudging the encyclopedia closer to order.

Wikipedia’s hierarchy is deliberately difficult to see. Editors work under pseudonyms. Articles appear collectively authored. There are no bylines, no salaries, no masthead. Pruitt was granted administrative privileges, after another editor nominated him through Wikipedia’s standard Request for Adminship process, where the editing community supported his candidacy. These privileges allow him to block users and close discussions, but he is careful about what that power does and does not mean. Wikipedia discourages editors from reverting—“undoing”—one another more than three times, regardless of correctness. “You can be blocked for twenty-four hours,” he said. “It doesn’t matter if you’re right.” He likes the rule. “It keeps things from turning personal.”

Inside Wikipedia, reputation accrues through time rather than visibility, and it “comes as much from longevity as anything else,” Pruitt said. “You stick around. People know you.”

Among the people who stick around—and who make consistent contributions to the site—are the Wiki-obsessives known colloquially as “super editors.” These individuals are responsible for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of edits. Although there are more than a hundred and thirty-two million registered accounts on Wikipedia, a study found that one per cent of these users are responsible for roughly eighty per cent of the site’s content.

Justin Knapp—a forty-three-year-old in Indiana who has held all sorts of jobs, including working at a pizzeria and at a crisis hotline—is one super editor. In 2012, he became the first person to surpass a million edits on the English-language Wikipedia, before Pruitt surpassed him in total edit count a few years later. Knapp told me that he doesn’t see Pruitt as a rival. “It’s not competition,” he said. “We’re collaborators. We’re colleagues.” Asked whether editors are motivated by metrics at all, Knapp was unequivocal: “I really don’t think the kind of person who sets about to spend his free time writing an encyclopedia is really the kind of person who cares a lot about being a big fish in a small pond.”

That ethos—low ego, high volume—helps explain how the site functions. Both Pruitt and Knapp described Wikipedia less as a platform than as an ongoing negotiation among strangers. Editors coördinate through talk pages—discussion threads attached to every article, some of which run for years. Disputes accumulate on talk pages over phrasing, sourcing, whether a subject belongs at all, with many never resolving. A finished Wikipedia page reflects a momentary consensus, subject to revision as soon as someone decides to revisit it.

A Wikipedia page’s internal debates often center on matters far removed from public controversies. “The most contested topics within Wikipedia are not things about the broader culture wars,” Wales, the site’s co-founder, wrote in an e-mail. “Of course there are difficult topics in the world, but most of the work isn’t about that. We have robust debates about even very obscure matters. That isn’t a problem. It’s what it means to be Wikipedia.”

Those debates unfold under unusual conditions. Anonymity shapes that process. Because editors generally operate under pseudonyms, an argument succeeds not on the strength of someone’s credentials or professional status but on its evidence and adherence to Wikipedia’s policies. Authority emerges slowly, through repeated participation. “You can’t force it,” Knapp said. “You earn it by being there.”

Pruitt is not known for winning disputes or shaping consensus through argument; he is known for his persistence. He fixes things quietly, avoids unnecessary fights, and doggedly returns to issues within an article that others have left behind. As Knapp said, “I think everyone agrees he’s a nice guy and does valuable things and is useful.” His scale of activity might suggest a certain level of influence over the site—he has altered millions of English-language Wikipedia articles—but the reality is more complicated. Wales wrote, “I just looked and this morning in the space of one minute he made 25 edits to remove a deprecated template parameter. He looks on pace to do hundreds of those in a day or two. That’s incredibly important, but hardly represents any sort of undue influence.”

That’s not to say that Pruitt doesn’t command an enormous amount of respect in the Wikipedia community. “We think of him as our No. 1 in amount of edits,” Rosie Stephenson-Goodknight, another super editor, told me. Stephenson-Goodknight, who is seventy-two years old, began editing Wikipedia in 2007, after looking up a defunct American publisher whose books she collected. “I thought there’d be a Wikipedia article,” she said. “And there wasn’t.”

Stephenson-Goodknight remembers double-checking the spelling of her search term. Nothing appeared. “It was that moment of clarity,” she said. “There is no Santa Claus. Mom and Dad are not infallible. Wikipedia does not have an article about everything.” So she decided to write one. “I started the article on Book League of America,” she said. “And it’s still there.”

Within a week or two, she wrote another. Then another. “I was hooked,” she explained. “It was like I was born to do this. There was just something about this researching and writing that just felt like it was me.” By 2014, she had become a super editor. Then, in December of that year, an academic paper quantified what editors like Stephenson-Goodknight had long suspected: just 15.53 per cent of English-language Wikipedia biographies were about women. A few months later, Stephenson-Goodknight launched a project called Women in Red, named for the red links that mark missing articles. The project focussed on creating Wikipedia articles about notable women. It has since produced hundreds of thousands of new entries.

In 2021, Stephenson-Goodknight was elected to the Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation, a position that she held through late 2024. Her tenure coincided with a fundamental shift in the role that Wikipedia plays on the internet. As the site entered its third decade, and artificial-intelligence algorithms grew hungry for data to learn on, Wikipedia articles were no longer just read; they were scraped, summarized, licensed, and folded into systems designed to answer questions elsewhere. In other words, Wikipedia had become infrastructure.

Pruitt was vaguely aware of the change before he fully grasped its implications. “Friends in tech would mention it,” he recalled. “They’d say, ‘You know Wikipedia is being used for this now.’ ” He did not follow developments in A.I. closely. “I don’t understand half of what Silicon Valley does,” he said. What he does understand well is reference works.

In October, 2025, when Elon Musk’s company xAI launched Grokipedia, an A.I.-generated encyclopedia that is often compared to Wikipedia, Pruitt approached it the way he would any new compendium. He searched for articles on subjects he knew well, such as nineteenth-century opera singers. “They weren’t there,” he said.

But what unsettled him was not what was missing from Grokipedia but what was slightly off. “Nothing was exactly wrong, but it was just less right than I would have made it,” Pruitt said. He described reading an entry that repurposed information from Wikipedia while subtly distorting it. In one instance, the entry summarized part of a person’s life in a way that struck him as careless, describing a seven-year period as “brief.” “I don’t think that’s brief,” he said.

The problem, as Pruitt saw it, was not the errors themselves—there are plenty of mistakes on Wikipedia—but rather where the responsibility for those errors lay. “Wikipedia can be fixed,” he said. Errors are corrected publicly, and editors can debate them. Responsibility is shared, and each edit can be traced. Grokipedia, on the other hand, and A.I.-generated information more broadly, obscured the information-gathering process. It generated text that sounded authoritative without revealing exactly how it arrived there. “It sounds right,” he said. “And that’s worse.”

Inside Wikipedia, the response was pragmatic. Editors clarified existing policy. The use of large language models to generate contributions or rewrite content became grounds for blocking users. The decision wasn’t simply ideological. “You can’t collaborate with something that doesn’t take responsibility,” Pruitt said. Responsibility, on Wikipedia, meant that every edit was logged, every disagreement archived, every change reversible.

Still, Wikipedia’s ban on A.I. doesn’t mean that A.I. is prevented from reusing content on Wikipedia. Multiple A.I. companies have acknowledged that they rely on Wikipedia as a source of training data and reference material, citing its scale and accessibility. The site’s content is openly available under a Creative Commons license, a feature long intended to encourage educational reuse but one that also made it especially legible to automated systems. Wikipedia became a foundational text for machine-learning models designed to summarize and answer questions using information drawn from other online sources. Analyses of A.I. outputs suggest that Wikipedia accounts for roughly a quarter of cited sources, according to data compiled by Semrush, a search-optimization company, with the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit that hosts Wikipedia, announcing earlier this year that Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral AI, and Perplexity had joined its commercial service for large-scale access to Wikimedia data.

Wales, Wikipedia’s co-founder, doesn’t see this as a big change in the way that the site was already functioning. In his view, the relationship between Wikipedia and the broader information ecosystem has always been cyclical rather than hierarchical. “Wikipedia informs journalists who then inform billions of people,” he wrote. “Wikipedia informs academics who then inform billions of people. And the journalists and academics (and artists and poets and everyone else!) inform Wikipedia. We’ve always been a layer.”

For Wales, the central question is how A.I. is used. “The key for me is ‘human in the loop,’ ” he wrote. “If you use AI in your work, that can be good or bad—it’s up to you to do it well. We don’t believe that at the current time, AI is anywhere good enough to directly write for Wikipedia without very careful human oversight.”

Midway through Wikipedia’s twenty-fifth year, the site remains dependent on human volunteers: editors like Pruitt, who are willing to spend thousands of hours making meticulous changes, and who insist that they could stop at any time. “I could,” Pruitt told me—stop, that is. “If I wanted to.” The statement wasn’t defiant; it was matter-of-fact. ♦

We’ve always been a layer.”For Wales, the central question is how A.I. is used. “The key for me is ‘human in the loop,’ ” he wrote. “If you use AI in your work, that can be good or bad—it’s up to you to do it well. We don’t believe that at the current time, AI is anywhere good enough to directly write for Wikipedia without very careful human oversight.”Midway through Wikipedia’s twenty-fifth year, the site remains dependent on human volunteers: editors like Pruitt, who are willing to spend thousands of hours making meticulous changes, and who insist that they could stop at any time. “I could,” Pruitt told me—stop, that is. “If I wanted to.” The statement wasn’t defiant; it was matter-of-fact. ♦A scientist with a Ph.D. from Harvard fatally shot three of her colleagues. Then revelations about her family history came to light.Carson Griffith, a former editor at Architectural Digest, covers business, wealth, and culture. She writes the newsletter “RPS” and has ghostwritten five books.

blocks.html_en: Today, much of Pruitt’s work is made possible by a specialized editing tool called AutoWikiBrowser. blocks.html_en: As I perched next to Pruitt in his den, he turned to the computer and began doing what he calls “mass editing.” He opened up a web-based external tool known as PetScan, which generates lists of Wikipedia articles by category, allowing him to layer categories the way a researcher might combine search terms. “Women scientists” crossed with “19th-century physicists,” for example, produces a list of biographies that fit both criteria, revealing pages that might be missing a relevant classification.

blocks.html_en: The method depends on intersections. Categories are layered together until they produce a set of pages that can be worked through in sequence. Too broad, and the list becomes unusable; too narrow, and it returns almost nothing. After Pruitt ran the query for “19th-century women physicists,” a list of articles appeared. blocks.html_en: Wikipedia’s hierarchy is deliberately difficult to see. Editors work under pseudonyms. Articles appear collectively authored. There are no bylines, no salaries, no masthead. Pruitt was granted administrative privileges, after another editor nominated him through Wikipedia’s standard Request for Adminship process, where the editing community supported his candidacy. These privileges allow him to block users and close discussions, but he is careful about what that power does and does not mean. Wikipedia discourages editors from reverting—“undoing”—one another more than three times, regardless of correctness. “You can be blocked for twenty-four hours,” he said. “It doesn’t matter if you’re right.” He likes the rule. “It keeps things from turning personal.”

sentences.en: There are no bylines, no salaries, no masthead.

sentences.en: Pruitt was granted administrative privileges, after another editor nominated him through Wikipedia’s standard Request for Adminship process, where the editing community supported his candidacy.
sentences.zh: 在另一位编辑通过维基百科的标准管理请求流程提名普鲁特后，普鲁特获得了管理特权，编辑社区支持他的候选资格。

sentences.en: These privileges allow him to block users and close discussions, but he is careful about what that power does and does not mean.

sentences.en: Wikipedia discourages editors from reverting—“undoing”—one another more than three times, regardless of correctness.
sentences.zh: 维基百科不鼓励编辑者相互恢复（“撤消”）次数超过三次，无论其正确性如何。

sentences.en: “You can be blocked for twenty-four hours,” he said.

sentences.zh: “如果你是对的，那并不重要。”

sentences.en: He likes the rule.

sentences.en: “It keeps things from turning personal.”
sentences.zh: “这可以防止事情变得个人化。”

blocks.html_en: Inside Wikipedia, reputation accrues through time rather than visibility, and it “comes as much from longevity as anything else,” Pruitt said. “You stick around. People know you.”

sentences.en: Inside Wikipedia, reputation accrues through time rather than visibility, and it “comes as much from longevity as anything else,” Pruitt said.

blocks.html_en: Among the people who stick around—and who make consistent contributions to the site—are the Wiki-obsessives known colloquially as “super editors.” These individuals are responsible for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of edits. Although there are more than a hundred and thirty-two million registered accounts on Wikipedia, a study found that one per cent of these users are responsible for roughly eighty per cent of the site’s content.

blocks.html_en: Justin Knapp—a forty-three-year-old in Indiana who has held all sorts of jobs, including working at a pizzeria and at a crisis hotline—is one super editor. In 2012, he became the first person to surpass a million edits on the English-language Wikipedia, before Pruitt surpassed him in total edit count a few years later. Knapp told me that he doesn’t see Pruitt as a rival. “It’s not competition,” he said. “We’re collaborators. We’re colleagues.” Asked whether editors are motivated by metrics at all, Knapp was unequivocal: “I really don’t think the kind of person who sets about to spend his free time writing an encyclopedia is really the kind of person who cares a lot about being a big fish in a small pond.”

blocks.html_en: That ethos—low ego, high volume—helps explain how the site functions. Both Pruitt and Knapp described Wikipedia less as a platform than as an ongoing negotiation among strangers. Editors coördinate through talk pages—discussion threads attached to every article, some of which run for years. Disputes accumulate on talk pages over phrasing, sourcing, whether a subject belongs at all, with many never resolving. A finished Wikipedia page reflects a momentary consensus, subject to revision as soon as someone decides to revisit it.

sentences.en: That ethos—low ego, high volume—helps explain how the site functions.
sentences.zh: 这种精神——低自我、高容量——有助于解释该网站的运作方式。

blocks.html_en: A Wikipedia page’s internal debates often center on matters far removed from public controversies. “The most contested topics within Wikipedia are not things about the broader culture wars,” Wales, the site’s co-founder, wrote in an e-mail. “Of course there are difficult topics in the world, but most of the work isn’t about that. We have robust debates about even very obscure matters. That isn’t a problem. It’s what it means to be Wikipedia.”

sentences.en: It’s what it means to be Wikipedia.”
sentences.zh: 这就是维基百科的意义。”

blocks.html_en: Those debates unfold under unusual conditions. Anonymity shapes that process. Because editors generally operate under pseudonyms, an argument succeeds not on the strength of someone’s credentials or professional status but on its evidence and adherence to Wikipedia’s policies. Authority emerges slowly, through repeated participation. “You can’t force it,” Knapp said. “You earn it by being there.”

sentences.en: Those debates unfold under unusual conditions.

sentences.en: Anonymity shapes that process.

sentences.en: Because editors generally operate under pseudonyms, an argument succeeds not on the strength of someone’s credentials or professional status but on its evidence and adherence to Wikipedia’s policies.
sentences.zh: 由于编辑通常使用假名，因此争论的成功不是取决于某人的资历或专业地位，而是取决于其证据和对维基百科政策的遵守。

sentences.en: Authority emerges slowly, through repeated participation.
sentences.zh: 通过反复参与，权威慢慢出现。

sentences.en: “You can’t force it,” Knapp said.
sentences.zh: “你不能强迫它，”纳普说。

sentences.zh: “你通过在那里获得它。”

blocks.html_en: Pruitt is not known for winning disputes or shaping consensus through argument; he is known for his persistence. He fixes things quietly, avoids unnecessary fights, and doggedly returns to issues within an article that others have left behind. As Knapp said, “I think everyone agrees he’s a nice guy and does valuable things and is useful.” His scale of activity might suggest a certain level of influence over the site—he has altered millions of English-language Wikipedia articles—but the reality is more complicated. Wales wrote, “I just looked and this morning in the space of one minute he made 25 edits to remove a deprecated template parameter. He looks on pace to do hundreds of those in a day or two. That’s incredibly important, but hardly represents any sort of undue influence.”

blocks.html_en: That’s not to say that Pruitt doesn’t command an enormous amount of respect in the Wikipedia community. “We think of him as our No. 1 in amount of edits,” Rosie Stephenson-Goodknight, another super editor, told me. Stephenson-Goodknight, who is seventy-two years old, began editing Wikipedia in 2007, after looking up a defunct American publisher whose books she collected. “I thought there’d be a Wikipedia article,” she said. “And there wasn’t.”

Mom and Dad are not infallible. Wikipedia does not have an article about everything.” So she decided to write one. “I started the article on Book League of America,” she said. “And it’s still there.”

blocks.html_en: Within a week or two, she wrote another. Then another. “I was hooked,” she explained. “It was like I was born to do this. There was just something about this researching and writing that just felt like it was me.” By 2014, she had become a super editor. Then, in December of that year, an academic paper quantified what editors like Stephenson-Goodknight had long suspected: just 15.53 per cent of English-language Wikipedia biographies were about women. A few months later, Stephenson-Goodknight launched a project called Women in Red, named for the red links that mark missing articles. The project focussed on creating Wikipedia articles about notable women. It has since produced hundreds of thousands of new entries.

blocks.html_en: In 2021, Stephenson-Goodknight was elected to the Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation, a position that she held through late 2024. Her tenure coincided with a fundamental shift in the role that Wikipedia plays on the internet. As the site entered its third decade, and artificial-intelligence algorithms grew hungry for data to learn on, Wikipedia articles were no longer just read; they were scraped, summarized, licensed, and folded into systems designed to answer questions elsewhere. In other words, Wikipedia had become infrastructure.

sentences.en: In 2021, Stephenson-Goodknight was elected to the Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation, a position that she held through late 2024.
sentences.zh: 2021 年，斯蒂芬森-古德奈特当选为维基媒体基金会董事会成员，并一直担任该职位至 2024 年底。

blocks.html_en: Pruitt was vaguely aware of the change before he fully grasped its implications. “Friends in tech would mention it,” he recalled. “They’d say, ‘You know Wikipedia is being used for this now.’ ” He did not follow developments in A.I. closely. “I don’t understand half of what Silicon Valley does,” he said. blocks.html_en: In October, 2025, when Elon Musk’s company xAI launched Grokipedia, an A.I.-generated encyclopedia that is often compared to Wikipedia, Pruitt approached it the way he would any new compendium. He searched for articles on subjects he knew well, such as nineteenth-century opera singers. “They weren’t there,” he said.

sentences.en: He searched for articles on subjects he knew well, such as nineteenth-century opera singers.

blocks.html_en: But what unsettled him was not what was missing from Grokipedia but what was slightly off. “Nothing was exactly wrong, but it was just less right than I would have made it,” Pruitt said. In one instance, the entry summarized part of a person’s life in a way that struck him as careless, describing a seven-year period as “brief.” “I don’t think that’s brief,” he said.

blocks.html_en: The problem, as Pruitt saw it, was not the errors themselves—there are plenty of mistakes on Wikipedia—but rather where the responsibility for those errors lay. “Wikipedia can be fixed,” he said. Errors are corrected publicly, and editors can debate them. Responsibility is shared, and each edit can be traced. Grokipedia, on the other hand, and A.I.-generated information more broadly, obscured the information-gathering process. It generated text that sounded authoritative without revealing exactly how it arrived there. “It sounds right,” he said. “And that’s worse.”

content_html_zh:
史蒂文·普鲁伊特 (Steven Pruitt) 被广泛认为是最多产的维基百科编辑，他已对该网站进行了超过 600 万次编辑，进而悄悄地塑造了每个主要人工智能的原材料。 聊天机器人接受了训练。

July 30, 2026

史蒂文·普鲁特 (Steven Pruitt) 晚上都在找出大多数人从未注意到的错误，并进行修复，但几乎没有人感谢他。 他在弗吉尼亚州亚历山大市一栋联排别墅的办公桌前辛勤工作，周围都是书籍——这种杂乱的工作表明他与纸张有着长期的关系，而不是对屏幕的迷恋。 然而他的作品必然是数字化的；晚饭后，有时甚至是深夜，他使用台式电脑来纠正日期、清理语法、标准化类别，有时还会在免费的在线百科全书维基百科上撰写完整的人物传记。

当然，维基百科不是他的雇主。 和网站上的所有编辑一样，普鲁特是一名志愿者。 “在这一点上，我不会说我没有参与其中，”他告诉我。 “但这比工作的风险要低得多，因为如果我出了什么问题，修复起来相当容易。 我可以自己修好。 我可以利用自己的时间做自己想做的事。” 尽管如此，他仍然坚持一些规则：“我确实尝试每天至少进行一次编辑。”

普鲁特四十二岁，全职担任联邦政府的记录管理承包商。 2006年，从威廉玛丽学院毕业后，由于亚历山大的房地产价格昂贵，他搬回父母身边。 近年来，他帮助母亲照顾父亲。 （当我报道这个故事时，普鲁特的父亲去世了。） 事实上，普鲁特——这位在塑造英语维基百科方面比其他任何人都做出了更多贡献的人——的生活，从大多数外在标准来看，都是平淡无奇的。

根据公开统计，普鲁特对维基百科进行了超过六百万次编辑，并创建了三万多篇文章。 他被广泛认为是全世界最多产的维基百科人。 （“这取决于你如何计算，”他说。 “不同的工具计算不同的东西。”）2017 年，《时代》杂志将他列入互联网上最有影响力的人物名单。 但在维基百科的编辑、研究人员和狂热读者的小圈子之外，这种认可几乎没有得到认可。

在该网站上，他的用户名是 Ser Amantio di Nicolao，指的是贾科莫·普契尼的喜剧《贾尼·斯基基》中的一个小角色。 普鲁特对歌剧的兴趣是真诚的，但其华丽的表现却具有误导性。 他避免戏剧化，这意味着他尽可能避免为仍然活着的人撰写维基百科传记。 “我通常不会在时事领域做太多事情，”他告诉我。 “不仅因为风险太高，而且有时因为在某个特定时刻对某个主题进行大量编辑，以至于我可能需要五到十分钟才能完成一次编辑。” 他更喜欢他所谓的“相当不起眼的死者”的传记。

“他们已经解决了，”他解释道。

2001 年，互联网企业家吉米·威尔士 (Jimmy Wales) 和哲学家拉里·桑格 (Larry Sanger) 推出了维基百科，作为协作知识创造的实验，允许任何拥有互联网连接的人做出贡献。 Pruitt 第一次接触这个网站是在 2003 年，当时他还在上大学。 “我不太明白那是什么，”他回忆道。

一年多的时间里，他根本没有编辑过。 他会通过搜索结果或链接偶然发现维基百科页面，然后继续前进。 不过，从 2004 年底到 2005 年初，他与该网站的关系开始发生变化。 百科全书已经达到了他所说的临界质量：“网站上有足够的东西，总有事情可做，”他说。 “但这不仅仅是一张白纸。” 差异很重要。 一本完全空洞的百科全书令人生畏。部分填写的内容需要修正和扩展。

普鲁特的一些最初的贡献与独立战争的小众方面有关，包括他自己的祖先之一的条目，一位来自弗吉尼亚州的相对默默无闻的士兵。 他写了几篇关于主题和人物的文章，比如弗朗西斯·萨尔瓦多，第一个在独立战争中被杀的犹太人，这些文章不太可能出现在传统的百科全书中，他惊讶地看着它们仍然存在，成为互联网上永久的一部分。 “到现在为止，已经二十多年了，”他说。

普鲁特在维基百科第一次大幅增长期间积极进行编辑。 2006 年，其英文版文章数量达到 100 万篇，这是一个里程碑，标志着其规模和合法性。 （维基百科现在有大约三百四十六种语言版本，其中英文版包含的条目最多。） 随着该网站变得越来越大、越来越突出，人们的期望也越来越强。 编辑不再是关于作者身份，而是更多关于管理职责。 “即使一篇文章看起来很完整，说实话，它也不是真正完整的，”普鲁特说。 每一页都处于临时状态，可以修改和争议。

随着时间的推移，普鲁特的工作从创建新文章转向改进现有文章。 他标准化了类别，修复了参考文献，并纠正了小错误，以免它们具体化为错误信息。 他仍然看到其中一些错误转移到互联网上的其他地方。 “你修复了一些东西，”他说，“然后你会在几年后看到它出现在其他地方。”

如今，普鲁特的大部分工作都是通过一种名为 AutoWikiBrowser 的专门编辑工具实现的。 它允许经验丰富的用户对大量文章进行快速、半自动编辑，标记常见问题并应用标准化修复。 普鲁特使用它进行大规模的修改，这是通过模拟方式无法实现的：更正日期、修复损坏的链接、标准化引文以及清理数千页的格式。 尽管有这个名字，“它不是自动的，”他说。 “你仍然需要审查每一个编辑。” 该工具不写文章，也不做判断。 它加快了维护速度。

当我坐在普鲁特的书房里时，他转向电脑，开始做他所谓的“大规模编辑”。 他开发了一个名为 PetScan 的基于网络的外部工具，该工具可以按类别生成维基百科文章列表，使他能够像研究人员组合搜索术语的方式对类别进行分层。 例如，“女科学家”与“19世纪物理学家”交叉，产生了符合这两个标准的传记列表，揭示了可能缺少相关分类的页面。

该方法取决于交叉点。 类别分层在一起，直到生成一组可以按顺序浏览的页面。 太宽泛，列表变得无法使用；太窄了，它几乎什么也没有返回。 普鲁特运行“19 世纪女性物理学家”查询后，出现了一个文章列表。 从那里开始，他行动迅速。 他打开一本传记，检查分类是否正确。 在某些情况下，一篇关于十九世纪女物理学家的文章被标记为科学家，而不是物理学家。 许多条目只需要进行少量修改即可；其他人需要更实质性的改变。 这项工作由快速连续做出的小决定组成，每一个决定都使百科全书更加接近秩序。

维基百科的层次结构故意让人难以理解。 编辑均使用化名。 文章显示为集体撰写。 没有署名、没有薪水、没有报头。 在另一位编辑通过维基百科的标准管理请求流程提名普鲁特后，普鲁特获得了管理特权，编辑社区支持他的候选资格。 这些特权使他能够阻止用户并关闭讨论，但他对这种权力的含义和不含义非常谨慎。 维基百科不鼓励编辑者相互恢复（“撤消”）次数超过三次，无论其正确性如何。 “你可能会被封锁二十四小时，”他说。 “如果你是对的，那并不重要。” 他喜欢这个规则。 “这可以防止事情变得个人化。”

普鲁特说，在维基百科内部，声誉是通过时间而不是知名度来积累的，它“与其他任何东西一样来自长寿”。 “你留下来。 人们认识你。”

在那些留下来并为该网站做出持续贡献的人中，有一些维基迷，俗称“超级编辑”。 这些人负责数十万甚至数百万次编辑。 尽管维基百科上有超过 1.32 亿个注册帐户，但一项研究发现，其中 1% 的用户负责该网站大约 80% 的内容。

贾斯汀·纳普 (Justin Knapp) 是一位超级编辑，现年 43 岁，来自印第安纳州，从事过各种工作，包括在比萨饼店和危机热线工作。 2012 年，他成为英语维基百科编辑次数超过 100 万次的第一人，几年后普鲁特的总编辑次数超过了他。 纳普告诉我，他不认为普鲁特是竞争对手。 “这不是竞争，”他说。 “我们是合作者。 我们是同事。” 当被问及编辑是否完全受到指标的激励时，纳普毫不含糊地说道：“我真的不认为那种打算利用业余时间编写百科全书的人真的是那种非常关心自己是小池塘里的大鱼的人。”

这种精神——低自我、高容量——有助于解释该网站的运作方式。 普鲁特和纳普都认为维基百科与其说是一个平台，不如说是陌生人之间正在进行的谈判。 编辑们通过讨论页进行协调——每篇文章都附有讨论线索，其中一些讨论会持续多年。 关于措辞、来源、主题是否属于主题的争议在讨论页面上不断积累，其中许多争议从未得到解决。 完成的维基百科页面反映了暂时的共识，一旦有人决定重新访问它，就会进行修改。

维基百科页面的内部辩论通常集中在远离公众争议的问题上。 “维基百科中最具争议的话题并不是更广泛的文化战争，”该网站的联合创始人威尔士在一封电子邮件中写道。 “世界上当然有困难的话题，但大部分工作都与此无关。 即使是非常晦涩难懂的问题，我们也会进行激烈的辩论。 那不是问题。 这就是维基百科的意义。”

这些辩论是在不寻常的条件下展开的。 匿名塑造了这个过程。 由于编辑通常使用假名，因此争论的成功不是取决于某人的资历或专业地位，而是取决于其证据和对维基百科政策的遵守。 通过反复参与，权威慢慢出现。 “你不能强迫它，”纳普说。 “你通过在那里获得它。”

普鲁特并不以通过争论赢得争议或达成共识而闻名。他以坚持不懈而闻名。 他悄悄地解决问题，避免不必要的争吵，并顽强地回到其他人留下的文章中的问题。 正如纳普所说，“我认为每个人都认为他是一个好人，做了有价值的事情并且很有用。” 他的活动规模可能表明对该网站有一定程度的影响力——他修改了数百万篇英文维基百科文章——但现实更为复杂。 威尔士写道：“我刚刚看了一眼，今天早上他在一分钟内进行了 25 次编辑，删除了一个已弃用的模板参数。 他预计在一两天内完成数百次这样的工作。 这非常重要，但几乎不代表任何不当影响。”

这并不是说普鲁特在维基百科社区中没有赢得极大的尊重。 “我们认为他是我们的编辑量第一，”另一位超级编辑罗西·斯蒂芬森-古德奈特告诉我。 斯蒂芬森-古德奈特 (Stephenson-Goodknight) 现年 72 岁，在查找了一家已停业的美国出版商收集的书籍后，于 2007 年开始编辑维基百科。 “我以为会有一篇维基百科文章，”她说。 “但没有。”

斯蒂芬森-古德奈特记得仔细检查了她的搜索词的拼写。 什么也没有出现。 “那是一个清晰的时刻，”她说。 “没有圣诞老人。 爸爸妈妈也不是绝对正确的。 维基百科并没有一篇涵盖所有内容的文章。” 于是她决定写一篇。 “我在美国图书联盟上开始写这篇文章，”她说。 “而且它还在那里。”

一两周内，她又写了一篇。 然后是另一个。 “我被迷住了，”她解释道。 “就好像我生来就是为了做这件事一样。 这种研究和写作的感觉就像是我自己。” 到2014年，她已经成为一名超级编辑。 然后，当年 12 月，一篇学术论文量化了斯蒂芬森-古德奈特等编辑长期以来的怀疑：只有 15.53% 的英文维基百科传记是关于女性的。 几个月后，斯蒂芬森-古德奈特启动了一个名为“红衣女性”的项目，该项目以标记缺失文章的红色链接命名。 该项目的重点是创建有关著名女性的维基百科文章。 此后，它已经制作了数十万个新条目。

2021 年，斯蒂芬森-古德奈特当选为维基媒体基金会董事会成员，并一直担任该职位至 2024 年底。 她的任期恰逢维基百科在互联网上扮演的角色发生根本性转变。 随着该网站进入第三个十年，人工智能算法越来越渴望学习数据，维基百科文章不再只是阅读；它们被抓取、总结、许可并合并到旨在回答其他地方问题的系统中。 换句话说，维基百科已经成为基础设施。

普鲁特在完全理解其含义之前就隐约意识到了这一变化。 “科技界的朋友会提到这一点，”他回忆道。 “他们会说，‘你知道维基百科现在正被用来做这件事。’”他没有关注人工智能的发展。 密切。 “硅谷所做的事情我有一半都不懂，”他说。 他最了解的是参考书。

2025 年 10 月，当埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 的公司 xAI 推出了 Grokipedia（一部人工智能生成的百科全书，经常与维基百科进行比较）时，普鲁特以对待任何新纲要的方式对待它。 他搜索有关他熟悉的主题的文章，例如十九世纪的歌剧歌手。 “他们不在那里，”他说。

但令他不安的不是 Grokipedia 缺少的内容，而是略有偏差的内容。 普鲁特说：“没有什么是完全错误的，但它只是比我想象的更不正确。” 他描述了自己读到的一个条目，该条目重新利用了维基百科的信息，同时巧妙地歪曲了它。 在一个例子中，该条目以一种让他觉得粗心的方式总结了一个人的部分生活，将七年描述为“短暂的”。 “我认为这并不简短，”他说。

正如普鲁特所见，问题不在于错误本身——维基百科上有很多错误——而在于这些错误的责任所在。 “维基百科是可以修复的，”他说。 错误会公开更正，编辑可以对其进行辩论。 责任共担，每次编辑都可追溯。 另一方面，Grokipedia 以及更广泛的人工智能生成的信息掩盖了信息收集过程。 它生成的文本听起来很权威，但没有透露它是如何到达那里的。 “听起来不错，”他说。 “那更糟了。”

维基百科内部的反应是务实的。 编辑澄清了现有政策。 使用大型语言模型来生成贡献或重写内容成为阻止用户的理由。 这个决定不仅仅是意识形态上的。 “你无法与不承担责任的人合作，”普鲁特说。 在维基百科上，责任意味着每一次编辑都会被记录，每一次分歧都会被存档，每一次更改都是可逆的。

尽管如此，维基百科对人工智能的禁令仍然存在。 并不意味着 A.I. 禁止重复使用维基百科上的内容。 多重人工智能 公司承认，他们依赖维基百科作为培训数据和参考材料的来源，理由是维基百科的规模和可访问性。 该网站的内容在知识共享许可下公开提供，这一功能长期以来旨在鼓励教育重用，但也使其对自动化系统特别清晰。 维基百科成为机器学习模型的基础文本，旨在使用从其他在线资源获取的信息来总结和回答问题。 人工智能分析 根据搜索优化公司 Semrush 与托管维基百科的非营利组织维基媒体基金会汇编的数据，结果表明维基百科约占引用来源的四分之一。今年早些时候，亚马逊、Meta、微软、Mistral AI 和 Perplexity 已加入其商业服务，以大规模访问维基媒体数据。

维基百科的联合创始人威尔士并不认为这对该网站已经运作的方式有很大的改变。 在他看来，维基百科与更广泛的信息生态系统之间的关系始终是循环的而不是层级的。 “维基百科为记者提供信息，然后记者又为数十亿人提供信息，”他写道。 “维基百科为学者提供信息，然后又为数十亿人提供信息。 还有记者和学者（还有艺术家、诗人和其他所有人！） 告知维基百科。 我们一直是一个层次。”

对于威尔士来说，核心问题是人工智能如何 被使用。 “对我来说，关键是‘人在循环中’，”他写道。 “如果你在工作中使用人工智能，这可能是好是坏——这取决于你能否做得好。 我们认为，目前人工智能还不足以在没有非常仔细的人类监督的情况下直接为维基百科撰写文章。”

维基百科已进入二十五年的中期，该网站仍然依赖于人类志愿者：像普鲁特这样的编辑，他们愿意花费数千小时进行细致的更改，并坚持认为他们可以随时停止。 “我可以，”普鲁特告诉我——停下来，就是这样。 “如果我愿意的话。” 这句话并没有挑衅的意思；这是事实。 ❖
